## This round: plan 2c Phase C, "Before C3" — the graph tier joins the bench

`lab/research/2026-09-28-graph-index-scale.md` §5 called for extending this bench with graph-tier ops once
`src/ledger/graph.ts` landed (plan 2c C3, commits `683b573`/`5eba173` on this branch) — the doc's own prior
round left a placeholder note ("Graph tier: not in this doc yet") instead of stubbing numbers. It's real now:
four new rows below (`graphRebuild`, `graphCatchup50`, `problemCountsTop20`, `traverseDepth4`), each mapped to
one of §5's four stated targets at 100k runs. See "Graph tier: against the §5 targets" further down for the
full readout — short version: `problemCountsTop20` comfortably clears its target; `graphCatchup50` clears on
p50 but not p95; `graphRebuild` and `traverseDepth4` both miss theirs, and a likely cause is proposed there
(not fixed here — `src/ledger/graph.ts` belongs to a different piece of plan 2c Phase C).

To make `traverseDepth4` a meaningful measurement at all, `scripts/bench-ledger.ts`'s own ledger generator
(`generateRealisticLedger`) now also emits a `wise.uses` C4 chain per run (2-4 edges, `component:hub-component
-> component:comp-<i> -> ... -> code:comp-<j>`, the middle/leaf parts drawn from a bounded, heavy-tailed
300-entry component pool) plus `wise.touches`/`wise.blast`, matching the research doc's own §5 suggestion ("a
few hundred components, heavy-tailed"). Every run's chain starts at the same fixed hub component
(`hub-component`) so the traversal bench always has a real, guaranteed-to-exist, heavily-reused start node —
see "Graph tier" below for why that choice also makes this a genuine stress case, not an artificially easy one.

The hot-tier rows below are simply this round's fresh re-measurement of the same ops the prior round's fix
(`bcc001f`) already validated — nothing in `src/ledger/index.ts` or the bench's hot-tier code changed this
round; only the graph-tier ops and the generator's new `wise.uses`/`touches`/`blast` fields were added.

## Bottom line (prior round): plan 2c Phase C, "before C3" — the catch-up O(n)

`lab/research/2026-09-28-graph-index-scale.md` §1 measured `catchup1` growing with ledger size (91.8 ms at
10k → 431.2 ms at 100k) and flagged it as a bug to find and fix before building the graph tier on top of the
same catch-up path. **Found (prior round): it was never in `src/ledger/index.ts` — it was a bug in this bench
script.**

`benchCatchUp` measured its per-sample closure through `timeCalls`, a generic helper that times its OWN
wall-clock span around calling the closure. The closure separately computed its own `ms` (wrapping only the
`nextRunNumber` call) and `return`ed it — but `timeCalls` never reads a callback's return value, it only
records how long the whole call took. So every reported `catchup1`/`catchup50` sample was actually timing:
copy the fixture's log + index.db into a fresh temp dir (fsynced) → append → fsync → the real catch-up →
`rmSync` the whole temp dir recursively. Copying and deleting O(n) bytes of fixture data on every single
sample is exactly what made the row grow with n — the real catch-up call buried inside it was never the thing
being measured. Fixed by timing `nextRunNumber` directly, not through `timeCalls`'s generic wrapper — see
commit `bcc001f` for the full writeup. `src/ledger/index.ts` itself was not touched; there was no real O(n) to
fix. This round's new `benchGraphCatchUp` (for the graph tier) follows the same fixed pattern from the start:
the timer wraps only `refreshGraph`, never the copy/append/fsync/cleanup around it.

## Graph tier: against the §5 targets

At **100,000 runs** (the only size that matters for the stated targets):

| target (§5) | row | measured (p50 / p95) | met? |
|---|---|---|---|
| graph rebuild < 30 s | `graphRebuild` | 42.15 s (1 sample) | **No** — ~1.4x over |
| graph catch-up of 50 runs < 200 ms | `graphCatchup50` | 141.0 ms / 276.7 ms | Partial — p50 clears it, p95 doesn't |
| `problemCounts` top-20 < 100 ms | `problemCountsTop20` | 8.3 ms / 12.5 ms | **Yes**, comfortably |
| depth-4 traversal < 100 ms | `traverseDepth4` | 778.5 ms / 1088.7 ms | **No** — ~8x over |

At **10,000 runs**, all four are comfortably under their 100k targets (`graphRebuild` 3.7 s, `graphCatchup50`
36-45 ms, `problemCountsTop20` ~1.1-1.3 ms, `traverseDepth4` 85-90 ms) — `traverseDepth4` in particular clears
its target at 10k but misses it at 100k, which is itself a finding: its cost is not growing gracefully with n.

**A likely (not confirmed, not fixed — `src/ledger/graph.ts` is a different piece of plan 2c Phase C, not
touched by this task) shared cause for the `graphRebuild` and `traverseDepth4` misses:** `triples`'s primary
key is `(p, s, o, run)` — `run` included by design, so the *same* logical edge (say, `hub-component`'s `uses`
edge to whatever mid-component a given run's chain picks) gets one **distinct physical row per witnessing
run**, not deduped down to one row per `(p,s,o)`. This bench's generator makes every single one of the 100,000
runs touch the same fixed hub component as `chainParts[0]`, so `hub-component` alone accumulates on the order
of 100,000 triples rows by the time `graphRebuild` finishes — a deliberately extreme, but not implausible,
"everyone imports the shared util module" fan-in. `traverse`'s `WITH RECURSIVE` walk expands every frontier
node via `triples WHERE t.s = walk.node` (any predicate) each hop; the schema's only index,
`idx_triples_pos (p, o, s)`, is shaped for predicate+object lookups (the inbound direction), not for "every
outgoing edge from this node regardless of predicate" — the exact access pattern `traverse`'s outbound step
needs. That mismatch would explain both why `graphRebuild` (which does ~100k inserts against a growing,
increasingly hub-heavy table) and `traverseDepth4` (which does a `t.s = walk.node` scan from that same
hub) both slow down superlinearly with n, while `problemCountsTop20` (a plain join over the *hot* tier's
already-indexed `categories`/`places` tables, never touching `triples` at all) stays fast. Flagging this for
whoever picks up plan 2c's rollup/index work next, not fixing it here.

## 1,000,000: extrapolated, not measured

Not run this round either — out of scope (10k and 100k only), and Task 27's own finding still applies:
`toJsonl`-shaped generation runs into Node's `buffer.constants.MAX_STRING_LENGTH` (≈512 MiB) somewhere north
of ~500,000 records on this build. Hot-tier catch-up cost is expected to stay flat at 1M the same way it did
10k→100k here. The graph tier's `graphRebuild`/`traverseDepth4` numbers above already show superlinear growth
10k→100k, so no flat extrapolation is offered for those two at 1M — see the root-cause note above.

## Rebuild / maintenance cadence

Unchanged from prior rounds' own finding for the hot tier: no proactive, size-triggered rebuild is needed — a
SQL table's rows grow proportionally with the ledger, and a catch-up only ever touches the bytes actually
added since the last one. The self-heal triggers (missing, unreadable, a suspicious size that fails
quick_check, a schema-version mismatch, a log shorter than `upto`, or a fingerprint mismatch) are unchanged by
this round. The graph tier's own watermark (`graph_upto`) follows the same incremental-by-byte-offset idea
(`refreshGraph`'s header comment) — this round's numbers above are the first real measurement of what that
costs at scale, not a maintenance-cadence change.
